t.segment lasana norte@-22.2,-68.6:
Lasana is a place where the desert makes a promise and keeps it. A few kilometres north of the oasis village of Chiu-Chiu, in northern Chile, the Loa river, the only river that crosses the Atacama, cuts a green gorge through the dry hills, with fields of alfalfa, willows and bright reeds, and on a rocky hill above the water stand the ruins of a pukará, a pre-Hispanic fortress of stone walls and terraces. The people who lived here, the Atacameño, lived in the oasis for centuries, farming maize, quinoa and potatoes, and later the Inca arrived and built roads, storehouses and administrative posts. This section of the Qhapaq Ñan, part of the six-nation UNESCO listing of 2014, passes through the area.

I cannot tell you exactly where the Lasana Norte segment lies, but the broader landscape is clear and the archaeology is easy to reach. The nearby church at Chiu-Chiu, one of the oldest in the region, is made of adobe with a roof of cactus wood, and dates from the seventeenth century. It stands in a plain white square with a small cemetery, as quiet as the desert itself.

Calama, a city of about a hundred and forty thousand, is the working base for the great copper mines of the region, and it has every kind of service, including fuel, workshops, restaurants and hotels. Fill up there before leaving, as the distances are long. The road to San Pedro de Atacama, a hundred kilometres to the south-east, is paved and straight, with big skies and views of volcanoes, and trucks to the mines use the main roads, so give them room. The side road to Lasana is quieter, with some gravel.

The desert is dry and cold at night, hot in the day and bright at all hours, so bring sunglasses, sunscreen and a good jacket. The altitude here is about two thousand five hundred metres, enough to feel it on a hard walk. Autumn and spring are comfortable, and summer afternoons can bring a dusting of rain and wind. The silence in the gorge is the real souvenir.
t.subsection abra de chaupiyacolas capilla:
The Incas built a road across the Andes, and in the north of Argentina it still runs under the hooves of mules and the boots of walkers. The Qhapaq Nan, the Great Inca Road, was a network of some 30,000 kilometres linking the empire from Colombia to Chile and Argentina, and parts of it were inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2014 across six countries. The segment of Chaupiyaco to Las Capillas, in the province of Salta, runs through the high valley of the Quebrada del Toro, one of the old routes between the Altiplano and the lowlands, and the section near Santa Rosa de Tastil follows the course used long before the Inca, by herders with llamas.

Santa Rosa de Tastil is the best-known archaeological site nearby, the remains of a town of stone houses on a terrace above the river, which flourished in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries before the Inca arrived. Hundreds of rooms, tombs and plazas can be seen, and a small museum next to the site houses the finds. The setting is magnificent, a wide, dry valley of red and ochre hills, with cardon cactus on the slopes, and the thin air at over three thousand metres has a bright, hard clarity.

The ride up Route 51 from Salta is spectacular. The road leaves the green valley of Lerma, climbs the Quebrada del Toro beside the river with tunnels, sharp bends and steep rock walls, and then climbs further toward the high plateau, the puna, passing the railway of the Train to the Clouds. The surface is mostly paved but with sections of damage, rockfall and gravel, and the altitude brings thin air, fierce sun, and temperatures that fall sharply at night. Wind is common, and sudden storms in summer can bring floods and landslides. The dry season, from April to October, is the best time, although nights can be freezing.

Santa Rosa de Tastil is a small place, and fuel is in Salta, in the lowlands, and in San Antonio de los Cobres, farther on, so fill up beforehand and carry extra. Altitude can bring headaches, so take it slowly, drink water and chew coca leaves if locals offer them, as they do. Empanadas and humitas are the local snacks.
t.segment turi norte@-22.2,-68.3:
The Inca built roads, and the greatest of them stretched down the Andes for thousands of kilometres. The Qhapaq Nan, the Andean road system, ran from Colombia to Chile and Argentina, linking farms, forts, storehouses and shrines, and UNESCO listed a large part of it in 2014. In northern Chile, segments of the road cross the Atacama Desert, one of the driest places on Earth, and the section near Turi is among the best preserved.

Turi lies on the edge of the high desert, about three thousand metres above sea level, above the Loa river canyon and close to Calama. Above the village is a pukara, a hilltop fortress of dry stone walls, which the Inca used to control the area. The road itself is a simple thing: a strip of cleared ground a few metres wide, edged by lines of stones, running in a straight line across the stony plain. In the desert, with almost no rain or wind erosion, it has survived for five hundred years. You can follow it for kilometres, and the line cuts straight over hills rather than around them.

There is no sizeable town on the list near the coordinates, so plan for self-sufficiency. Calama, the nearest big town, has fuel, workshops and hotels, and San Pedro de Atacama is the popular base to the southeast, with a good choice of places to eat and sleep. The paved road between them is excellent, but side tracks into the desert are often gravel and sand, and they can be rough. Altitude is serious, so take time to acclimatise and drink plenty of water. The sun is fierce, even in winter, and the nights are cold.

Light is the great reward. In the early morning and late afternoon, the stony hills turn rust, gold and violet, and the line of the road shows up clearly, running toward the snow-capped volcanoes on the horizon. The air is thin and dry and the sky is a deep blue. Respect the site by staying on tracks, and do not move stones. The road is a fragile thing, and it deserves the care.
t.parc national de masoala@-15.5,50.2:
Masoala is the great green thumb of Madagascar, a peninsula pushing into the Indian Ocean in the northeast of the island, and the national park that fills it is the biggest protected area in the country. The rainforest here comes down to the beach, and the border between trees and sea is almost nonexistent, so you can stand on white sand with palms behind you and coral in front. Antongil Bay, on the western side, is deep and wide, and humpback whales come there to breed between about July and September.

The wildlife is a roll call of Madagascar's strangest residents. The red ruffed lemur is found only on this peninsula, and lives high in the canopy, making loud, raucous calls. There are chameleons, leaf-tailed geckos, tomato frogs and countless orchids, and the aye-aye, the lemur with the spindly finger, is believed to live in the forest too, though it is rarely seen. Zurich Zoo even built a replica Masoala rainforest in a hall, which tells you how special the place is to naturalists.

There is no proper road through Masoala, which is part of what has protected it. Visitors come by boat from Maroantsetra or by tracks from the town of Antalaha, the centre of Madagascar's vanilla industry, and roads in the region are rough, often muddy and prone to washouts. The dry season from September to December is the most dependable time, and the cyclone season between January and March brings heavy rain and storm risk.

Be ready for self-sufficiency. Fuel is available only in the larger towns, and you will want to carry extra if you try overland travel. Local guides, who are required in the park, know the trails and keep you safe from stumbles and surprises. Take insect repellent, light waterproofs and good boots, and enjoy a cup of locally grown vanilla tea in the evening.
t.salta@-24.8,-65.4:
Salta calls itself La Linda, the beautiful, and the old centre makes a decent case for it. The city lies in a green valley in the far north-west of Argentina, about twelve hundred metres above the sea, with the Andes to the west and the humid forest edge to the east. The Spanish founded it in 1582, and the colonial core still shows it, with the cathedral's pink facade, the arcaded cabildo on the main plaza and the cafés underneath the verandahs. In the evening the plaza fills with families, buskers and street food, and the empanadas salteñas, small and juicy with beef, are an essential meal.

For riders, Salta is the gate to the Calchaquí valleys, a rugged landscape of red rock, dry river canyons and tall cactus. To the south the road heads through the Quebrada de las Conchas, a gorge of eroded sandstone with names like the Devil's Throat and the Amphitheatre, ending in the wine town of Cafayate, known for the white grape torrontés. To the west, the national route climbs the Cuesta del Obispo, a dirt and paved switchback pass that reaches well over three thousand metres, before dropping to the village of Cachi, with white adobe houses and a view of snow-capped Nevado de Cachi.

These are not routes for a bad day. Distances are large, altitude is real, and temperatures swing wildly between sun and shade. Sections of gravel appear without warning, and in the summer rainy season from December to March, flash floods can cut roads and wash out bridges for hours or days. Autumn and winter are drier and clearer, though nights at altitude go below freezing. Wind and dust are common, and animals wander onto the road.

Salta has all the fuel, workshops and food that a rider needs, so it is the place to prepare for the trip. Campo Quijano, at the start of the Quebrada del Toro, is the last sizeable town on the road toward the Andes, and the famous high railway, known as the Tren a las Nubes, passes along that gorge. After the ride, the peñas, folk music clubs with guitars and singing, are a pleasant way to wind down.
t.segment las peras sauzalito@-24.8,-66.1:
This stretch lies in the high valleys of Salta province, in the dry north-west of Argentina, and it belongs to the great Inca road system the Incas called Qhapaq Ñan. UNESCO listed the network in 2014, a web of tracks and stone-built stairways, bridges and storehouses reaching from Ecuador to central Chile, built to link a mountain empire with no wheeled carts. Messengers on foot, the chasqui, ran in relays along these routes, and llama caravans carried loads on the long climbs. Some stretches are still walkable, and sections survive near modern roads.

Do not expect a clearly marked spot here. This is a segment of road and country rather than a single monument, and the best way to understand it is to ride the valley around it. The terrain is high, dry and open, with cactus and thorny scrub on the slopes, bare ridges striped in red and ochre, and snow-capped peaks showing in the west on clear mornings. The Nevado de Cachi, over six thousand metres, dominates the skyline of this part of the Calchaquí region. Tracks and old roads wander through quebradas, narrow dry valleys that turn into raging streams after storms.

The riding is a mix. Main roads such as Ruta 40 in this area are partly paved and partly gravel, often slow and exposed to cross-winds, with surface that turns to washboard and loose stone. Side tracks need patience, good tyres and a sense of humour. Altitude matters, since you are riding at two to three thousand metres, where engines lose power and riders get headaches and shortness of breath. Drink water, take it slowly, and respect the weather, because afternoon storms can arrive out of a blue sky in summer.

Fuel is the main practical problem. Cachí, about thirty-four kilometres away, is a tiny place of two thousand people and may not have fuel when you need it, so fill the tank in a larger town such as Salta or Cafayate and carry extra if you can. Shops are sparse, and food is simple: empanadas, locro stew, goat cheese and maize. Nights are cold even in summer, and winter brings frost. The best seasons are autumn and spring, with clear light and steady weather.
t.segment camar sur@-23.4,-68.0:
Camar is a very small village on the high edge of the Atacama, at around two and a half thousand metres, south of the great Salar de Atacama and a long way from anywhere that sells fuel. Its Segment Camar Sur belongs to the Qhapaq Ñan, the road network that the Inca state laid across the Andes in the fifteenth century, and in this part of northern Chile, the road ran along the flanks of the volcanic range, linking oases and passes between the high plateau and the coast. UNESCO lists the system as a whole, a web that stretched some thirty thousand kilometres.

The Incas did not so much invent these paths as bind together older ones. Atacameño herders had led llama caravans along these ways for centuries, carrying salt, wool, dried meat and maize between the desert settlements and the highlands, and the Incas turned the tracks into an administered system with relay stations and storehouses, where officials and messengers could rest. A messenger could pass news along the whole empire in a few days by running in relays, handing the message from one runner to the next. In the desert, evidence of the road is often subtle: a line of cleared stones, a low retaining wall, a cairn at a pass.

For a rider, the Atacama is not about corners. Main roads are long, straight and almost empty, climbing and dropping in great steps between basins, and the colour of the land changes with the hour, from pale ochre to deep red. Side tracks run over sand, gravel and salt crust, and wind builds in the afternoon, so go early. The air is thin, and a loaded bike loses power at this height, so do not be surprised when it feels flat. Nights are cold, even in summer, often below freezing, and the stars are stunning.

The pin lists no nearby town, so plan the logistics carefully. San Pedro de Atacama is the nearest place with fuel, food and beds, and it is a long way off, so fill the tank there and carry a spare can. Bring plenty of water, a warm layer, a puncture kit and offline maps, and tell someone your plan. Spring and autumn bring stable weather, while summer afternoons can bring storms in the high country that send water down dry gullies with surprising speed.
t.segment camar sur@-23.5,-68.0:
Camar is the kind of place that is easy to miss and hard to forget. A cluster of low houses, a small chapel and a handful of green terraces watered by a stream sit on the high desert, with volcanoes standing on the horizon in every direction. This is the land of the Lickanantay, the Atacameño people, who have lived in this arid country for thousands of years and who still herd llamas and grow maize, alfalfa and beans on patches of irrigated land. Their name for the landscape includes an understanding of water that outsiders usually lack.

The surrounding country has a stark beauty. To the north lies the Salar de Atacama, a vast salt flat that glitters white in the sun, where flamingos feed in shallow lagoons. East of it rises Lascar, an active volcano at about fifty-six hundred metres, trailing a faint plume of steam on clear days. The high lagoons of Miscanti and Miñiques, a little way south-east, are a deep, still blue under a pale sky, ringed by golden grass, and they are among the finest sights of northern Chile. Vicuñas graze beside the road, and in the evening the light turns the hills to copper.

The road here is part of the old Inca route, and a segment of it, Camar Sur, is included in the UNESCO listing of the Qhapaq Ñan. Ride it for the landscape rather than for the corners. Long straights across the plateau alternate with climbs through volcanic hills, with magnificent views, little traffic and few signs. The altitude is a factor, since the thin air saps power from engines and energy from riders, so ride at a modest pace, drink plenty of water, and rest if you feel dizzy or have a headache.

Stars deserve a mention. This region has some of the clearest skies on earth, and an hour outside the village after dark, with the engine off and a jacket on, is a fine way to end a day. San Pedro de Atacama is the nearest town with fuel, food and accommodation, and it is well over an hour away. Plan fuel carefully, because the distances between stations are long and no one will sell you petrol in a village without a pump. Winter nights are bitter, summer afternoons can bring thunderstorms, and spring is mild and settled.
t.purmamarca@-23.7,-65.5:
Purmamarca is the village most people photograph first in the Quebrada de Humahuaca, and the reason is the hill behind it. The Cerro de los Siete Colores rises straight from the edge of the settlement in bands of pink, rust, ochre, green and grey, and the colours change hourly: pale and chalky at noon, deep and almost wet-looking when the low sun rakes across them in the late afternoon. It is a small adobe village, about two thousand three hundred metres up in Jujuy province, in the far north-west of Argentina.

The Quebrada itself is a long dry valley carved by the Rio Grande, and was a trade corridor long before the Spaniards or even the Inca arrived. Llama caravans carried salt, maize and textiles between the Andean highlands and the lowlands, and the route later became the road to Potosi and the silver. UNESCO listed the whole valley as a cultural landscape in 2003. In Purmamarca the little church, dedicated to Santa Rosa de Lima and dating to the eighteenth century, stands beside the square, where stalls sell woven goods, ponchos and carved cactus-wood bits and pieces. It gets busy with tour buses in the middle of the day and quiet again in the evening.

For riders the village is a short detour off Ruta 9, the main road up the Quebrada. Ruta 52 starts here and climbs west in a famous series of switchbacks, the Cuesta de Lipan, towards the Salinas Grandes and the border passes into Chile, so this is where a ride into the high Andes begins. Expect thin air, strong sun and sudden cold, and carry water; altitude can make you headachy even if you are only riding.

Fuel is the practical question. Purmamarca itself is tiny, and you should not count on finding petrol at the pump you need, so treat Tilcara, about twenty kilometres up the valley and the nearest place from the list with five thousand people, as your reliable stop, or fill in the provincial capital before you start. Food is simple and good: empanadas, humita, locro, quinoa dishes and the occasional llama stew, with a coca tea if the altitude is bothering you. Mornings are the best time, before the wind gets up and the tour groups arrive.
t.uyuni@-20.5,-66.8:
At 3,650 metres above sea level, on the high plateau of south-west Bolivia, Uyuni is a dusty, windblown frontier town that exists for one reason. Just beyond it lies the Salar de Uyuni, the largest salt flat in the world, a blinding white plain of more than ten thousand square kilometres, which formed when ancient lakes dried out. In the rainy season, from roughly January to March, a thin film of water turns the salt into a mirror that doubles the sky, and in the dry season the surface cracks into hexagonal plates that stretch to the horizon.

Uyuni itself is rough and ready. The railway reached it early in the twentieth century, and the cemetery of old steam locomotives on the edge of town, rusted and sprayed with graffiti, is a sad and photogenic reminder of the mining trade that once passed through. The streets are wide, the wind is cold even at midday, and nights can fall well below freezing. The altitude is a real factor, so take it slowly, drink water and avoid heavy meals if your head aches. Many travellers use the town to sort out supplies before heading into the high desert.

The ride towards Laguna Colorada, about two hundred kilometres to the south, is a different order of adventure. The tracks cross the salt flat, then climb across lava fields, past volcanoes, rocky valleys and lagoons that range from turquoise to green. The surface is gravel, sand and corrugations for most of the route, and wind, cold and altitude add to the challenge. Heights of four thousand five hundred metres or more are reached, and the red-hued Laguna Colorada, at about four thousand three hundred metres, is coloured by algae and minerals and ringed by flamingos feeding in the shallows. Because tracks branch and navigation is difficult, most people go with a guide, and the salt itself, particularly when wet, corrodes metal, so the bike needs a good wash afterwards.

Fuel is the thing that matters. Uyuni has petrol stations, though supplies sometimes run low, and prices for foreigners may differ from local rates, so ask. Beyond the town, there is almost none, so carry spare fuel, water, warm clothing, and food. Bring cash in bolivianos, since cards are rarely accepted. The sunrise over the salt, with a pale pink light creeping across the white and the cold biting at your fingers, is a memory that stays.
t.susques@-23.4,-66.4:
Susques is a small high-altitude town on the road to Chile, perched on the Argentine puna at about 3,600 metres, where the air is thin, the sky is deep blue and the horizon is made of bare rust-coloured hills. The Ruta 52 climbs here from Jujuy through the Quebrada de Purmamarca, over the Cuesta de Lipán, one of the highest and most dramatic mountain roads in Argentina, then crosses the great white Salinas Grandes, the salt flats, before arriving in Susques. The town marks the beginning of the real altiplano.

The riding is wild and wonderful, with wide, open bends, empty straights and long views over the plateau. Traffic is light, mainly trucks heading for the Paso de Jama and the Chilean border, and the main dangers are altitude, wind, cold nights and long distances between services. Take it slow on the high passes, drink plenty of water and be ready for headaches or breathlessness. The sun is fierce at this height, but temperatures drop sharply at night.

The little adobe church in Susques is one of its best sights. Built in colonial times, it has thick white walls and a roof made from the wood of the cardón cactus, a material that has stood up to the high Andes for centuries. The town is inhabited largely by Kolla and Atacama indigenous communities, who herd llamas and sheep, and weave wool in bright patterns. Vicuñas, wild relatives of the llama, graze the dry plains nearby, and you may see them in the early morning.

There is basic accommodation and food in Susques, simple but welcome, and a petrol station, though you should treat fuel as something to plan ahead rather than hope for. Carry a reserve and top up whenever you can, because the next services are far away. The Paso de Jama, at over four thousand metres, leads on to San Pedro de Atacama in Chile, and the border formalities are strict, so check opening hours and paperwork before you go.
t.san pedro de atacama@-22.9,-68.2:
San Pedro de Atacama is a small adobe town in the driest desert on Earth, and the contradiction is the attraction. It lies at 2,400 metres on the edge of the Salar de Atacama, a vast salt flat, in an oasis fed by streams from the Andes. The streets are dusty and low, the walls are the colour of dry mud, and behind the town the Licancabur volcano, nearly 5,920 metres, stands as a perfect cone on the border with Bolivia. Everything here seems to lean towards the sky.

The Lickanantay people have lived in this oasis for thousands of years, and the town's church, built in the eighteenth century of adobe, with a roof of cardón cactus wood, is still the centre of local life. Spanish arrived in the sixteenth century, and the village was a stop on the old routes between the Andes and the coast. Today its small main streets are lined with adobe restaurants, tour offices and hostels, and the evening air is full of guitar music and the smell of wood fire.

The surroundings are dramatic. To the south-west the Valle de la Luna, a landscape of salt-crusted ridges and sand dunes, glows orange at sunset, and further out, the El Tatio geysers steam in the cold dawn at 4,300 metres. Flamingos feed in the lagoons of the salar. The air is so dry and clear that it is one of the best places on Earth for stargazing, and the big astronomical observatories of the high desert are nearby. Nights are cold even after hot days.

Riding here is a thrill, but it demands preparation. The road to Argentina over the Paso de Jama climbs onto the altiplano at over 4,200 metres, through some of the emptiest, most beautiful country in South America, and altitude sickness is a real risk, so take it slowly and carry water. Distances are huge, and winds blow hard in the afternoon. The nearest big town, Calama, is about a hundred kilometres away. San Pedro has a fuel station, but supplies can run short, so fill up whenever you can, and carry a spare container if you are heading out of town. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.segment peine norte@-23.6,-68.0:
Peine is a village at the southern end of the Salar de Atacama, one of those small oases that makes the desert liveable, and the road that comes to it traverses some of the strangest country in Chile. At around 2,450 metres, it lies in a fold of the ground between the salt flat and the volcanic highlands, and its irrigated fields of alfalfa and its fruit trees stand out bright green against the brown hills. It is a Lickanantay community, and its stone church and its terraces, watered by channels that come down from the mountains, have been in use for centuries.

The Salar de Atacama is the largest salt flat in Chile, a crust of white and grey salt crystals that stretches across the basin, ringed by volcanic cones. Salt lakes at its edge are home to flamingos, three species of them, feeding on brine shrimp. At Laguna Chaxa, north of Peine, the birds stand in pink flocks in the shallows, with the cones of the Andes behind. To the east the Lascar volcano, at 5,592 metres, still sends up a thin plume of steam, and in the afternoon light the whole area glows with colour.

For the rider, the roads around Peine are long, straight and spectacular. Route 23 runs south from San Pedro along the salar, passing the villages of Toconao and Socaire, with views of volcanoes and salt flats, and leads on to the high lagoons of Miscanti and Miñiques above 4,000 metres. The surface is generally good, though gravel patches and drifting sand are common, and the wind can be fierce in the afternoon. At this altitude the air is thin, so expect your bike to run rough and take it easy yourself.

Plan carefully, because services are scarce. San Pedro de Atacama, roughly a hundred kilometres to the north, is the nearest place with a fuel station and a wider range of food, and if you are heading to the high lagoons it makes sense to fill up and carry extra. In the villages, small shops sell water, bread and simple meals, but hours are unpredictable. Nights are freezing even in summer, and the sun is brutal by day, so carry sunscreen and warm layers. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and it is best to start early.
t.sultan epe@44.5,51.0:
A mosque dug into the rock is a rare thing, and Sultan-Epe is one of the best. It lies on the Mangystau peninsula in western Kazakhstan, a stark region of chalk cliffs, canyons and salt flats stretching toward the Caspian Sea, and the mosque is cut into a hillside, with a low entrance leading down into a cool chamber. It is named after Sultan-Epe, a Sufi holy man revered in the region, and it forms part of a network of underground mosques and burial grounds that have been pilgrimage places for centuries.

Mangystau has a big history written into its rocks. The land was once the floor of an ancient sea, and fossils of shells and sharks' teeth lie scattered across the plains. Later it became a corridor for Silk Road caravans moving between the Caspian and Central Asia, and nomads buried their dead in great stone cemeteries marked with carved headstones and tombs shaped like small buildings. Pilgrims still make the journey to shrines such as this, and visitors are expected to dress modestly, remove their shoes at the entrance, and treat it as a sacred place.

The riding here is a long journey across wide, open land. The roads between settlements are mostly tarmac, but the tracks to the shrines are gravel and sand, and weather can turn them into a challenge. The nearest town in the data, Taūshyq, is thirty kilometres away and has only a few thousand people. The big regional centre is Aktau on the Caspian coast, and the small Caspian port of Fort-Shevchenko lies not far to the north-west. Fuel is scarce between towns, so fill up whenever you can and carry extra.

Summer is very hot and winters are cold with strong winds, so spring and autumn are better. In spring the steppe sometimes blooms with tulips, a surprise in such dry country. Take plenty of water, because you are a long way from help. The local people are hospitable and may offer tea and bread if you stop, and it is worth accepting.
t.abu dhabi@24.5,54.4:
Abu Dhabi sits on an island, joined to the mainland by bridges, and the flat green and white city that spreads across it grew from a fishing village with a fort. Qasr Al Hosn, the old white coral-and-sea-stone fort dating from the eighteenth century, still stands among the high-rises as the oldest building in the city, and it was the home of the ruling family before the oil era. Oil was found offshore in the late 1950s and exports began in the early 1960s, and when Sheikh Zayed became ruler he put much of the money into trees, roads and schools. In 1971, he became the first president of the United Arab Emirates.

The city's landmarks are on a huge scale. The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque, completed in 2007, has eighty-two white marble domes and a vast courtyard, and is open to visitors outside prayer times with modest dress. The Louvre Abu Dhabi, under a great perforated dome that scatters light like rain, opened in 2017. The Corniche is a long waterfront promenade with beaches and cycle paths, and Yas Island hosts the Formula One season finale. Beyond the city, the desert begins almost immediately, with red dunes and salt flats.

For riders, the roads are wide and fast, with smooth tarmac, many lanes and careful signage. Speed cameras are widespread, and the fines are heavy, so keep to the limits. The best riding is outside town, on the long highway to Al Ain, which passes through the desert with gentle curves, and on to the oasis at Al Qattara. Sand blows across the road in wind, and visibility can be reduced in a dust storm. Helmets are compulsory and licences are checked. Summer heat is brutal, so go early in the morning or between November and March.

Practically, fuel stations are everywhere and the price is moderate, and there are shops and cafes at every intersection. Water is essential, and a hydration pack is a good investment. The city has a full range of restaurants, from Emirati dishes such as machboos and luqaimat dumplings to every cuisine in the world. Parking for motorcycles is easy in most areas. If you leave the city for a long desert run, let someone know your route, carry a phone and fill the tank before leaving.
t.la quiaca@-22.1,-65.6:
La Quiaca is the last town in Argentina, and at about 3,400 metres above sea level it feels like it. The Puna plateau here is high, cold and windswept, with a sky of hard blue and a landscape of tawny grass and bare hills, and the border with Bolivia runs along a dry riverbed on the edge of town. A bridge crosses to Villazón, a bustling Bolivian town just two kilometres away. Argentine National Route 40, the long road that runs the length of the country along the Andes for more than five thousand kilometres, ends here, and a sign at the border marks the northern terminus.

The country is the Altiplano, home to llamas, vicuñas and quinoa farmers, with adobe houses, shawl-wearing women and the smell of wood smoke. Nearby, the Laguna de los Pozuelos draws flocks of flamingos, and to the south, the Quebrada de Humahuaca, a UNESCO-listed valley, opens up into colourful rock formations and old villages. Practically, La Quiaca has fuel stations, though supplies can be limited at times, and it is wise to fill up whenever you can. The town has simple hotels, restaurants serving empanadas, llama stew and hot soup, and small shops. Take layers, sun protection and plenty of water, and acclimatise gently before riding hard. t.abra del acay@-24.4,-66.2:
Abra del Acay is the highest point on Argentina's Ruta 40, at 4,895 metres, and one of the highest road crossings in the Americas. The pass lies in the province of Salta, on the road between San Antonio de los Cobres on the puna to the north and the village of Payogasta and the Calchaquí valley to the south. A motorcycle makes noticeably less power at this height, and carburetted engines run rich and sluggish while fuel-injected ones cope better but still feel strangled. The rider is no better off: headaches, short breath and clumsy thinking are normal, and stopping for ten minutes at the top is an excuse rather than a hardship. Drink plenty, eat lightly and do not hang around for the sunset. Take the pass in the middle of the day, when the wind is lowest and the surface thawed, and watch for ice patches in the shadow of the corners, even in summer. Snow can shut the road in winter, and storms can arrive from nowhere.

The road is a work of patience. From San Antonio de los Cobres, a small mining and railway town on the high plateau, the surface is mostly paved for a stretch and then gives way to gravel, in tight hairpins on the descent toward Payogasta. Traffic is thin. You may meet a truck or a pickup and more often a herd of vicuñas, the slender wild relatives of the llama, or a guanaco standing on a ridge as if posted there. Check conditions in San Antonio before you start.

History lies close by. The ruins of Santa Rosa de Tastil, a large pre-Inca settlement of stone houses on the quebrada, are a short way along the main road to the north, and the old route here was a path for llama caravans long before motorcycles, linking the puna with the valleys below. Fuel is the practical question: San Antonio de los Cobres has a pump, but carry a spare bottle, because queues and shortages are not unknown. Cachí, further south, is the better-stocked place to refuel, and the descent there passes through some of the most dramatic colour on the whole route.
t.salar de uyuni@-20.1,-67.5:
The Salar de Uyuni is the largest salt flat in the world, a sheet of white about ten thousand square kilometres in extent, lying high in the southwest of Bolivia at roughly 3,650 metres. It formed when prehistoric lakes dried up, and what remains is a crust of salt several metres thick, with brine beneath it. Under a hard sun the surface is blinding, and the horizon disappears, so that the land and sky merge, and distance becomes meaningless. It is one of the strangest places a rider can reach.

Riding on the salt is nothing like riding on a road. The surface is hard and flat, patterned with hexagonal ridges where the salt has dried, and in the dry season you can ride across it at speed in any direction. The difficulty is navigation. With no landmarks, you can lose your bearings, and a GPS or an experienced guide is essential. The glare calls for good sunglasses, and the sun at this altitude burns quickly. The wind can be fierce in the afternoon. In the wet season, from roughly December to March, a thin layer of water covers the flat and turns it into a vast mirror, which is lovely to see but treacherous to ride, as the water hides soft patches and corrodes the machine. Salt is brutal on a motorcycle, getting into brakes, chains and electrics, so wash the bike thoroughly with fresh water afterward.

There is a good deal to see. Isla Incahuasi, an island of fossilised coral rising from the salt, is covered in giant cacti, some of them centuries old. Hotels in the area are built partly of salt blocks, and the town of Colchani on the edge of the flat produces salt for sale. Beneath the salt lies one of the world's largest reserves of lithium, a metal that has made the place a topic in the global debate over batteries. The railway cemetery outside the town of Uyuni, where old locomotives rust in the desert, is another curiosity.

The practical points are serious. Fuel is available in Uyuni, and not out on the salt or on the tracks nearby, so fill up and carry extra. Water is vital, and so are warm layers, as the nights are freezing. Flamingos live in the high lakes to the south.
t.san antonio de los cobres@-24.2,-66.3:
San Antonio de los Cobres lies at about thirty-seven hundred metres in the Puna of Salta, a high, dry plateau in the north-west of Argentina where the sky is enormous and the air thin and clear. The town is small, with low adobe houses and a main street that looks across a bare valley to red and ochre hills, and it is the highest place of any size on the route that crosses the Andes toward Chile. t.la poma@-24.7,-66.2:
La Poma lies in the high valleys of Salta province, in north-west Argentina, at the northern end of the Calchaquí valleys and below the wall of the Andes, and it is one of the remotest places on Route 40. The altitude is well over three thousand metres, and the air is thin, cold and astonishingly clear.

The surface is rough, the gradients are steep, and the weather is wild, with snow possible at any time of year. The landscape is the high Andean desert, a world of rock, sand and sparse grass, with colourful mountains in shades of red, yellow and grey. Vicuñas, wild relatives of the llama, graze on the high ground, and condors circle overhead. Nevado de Acay, a glaciated peak of more than five thousand metres, stands above the pass. Check the road status before you start, as it is closed after snow or rain. A basic breakfast and a coca-leaf tea at a village house is a good start to the day.
t.tilcara@-23.6,-65.4:
Tilcara sits at about 2,400 metres in the Quebrada de Humahuaca, the long, colourful gorge in Jujuy province that was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003. The town is a small place of low adobe houses and cobbled streets, with a plaza, a church with a white bell tower and a scattering of craft shops and cafes, and it is surrounded by hills striped in red, ochre, pink and green. The air is dry and sharp, the sun is strong, and the sky is a deep, dark blue at midday.

The people who lived here, called the Tilcara, farmed the terraces and defended themselves from this site, and later the Incas took control. The ruins have been partly reconstructed, and from the top, the view up and down the valley is wide, with the river braided across a gravel bed and fields of maize and quinoa below. Mornings are cold, with frost in winter, but midday can be hot. Take sun protection, water and warm clothes for the evenings.

Tilcara has fuel, ATMs and plenty of places to eat, which makes it a comfortable base. The nearby villages of Maimará, known for its Painter's Palette hill, and Purmamarca, with its Hill of Seven Colours, are easy to reach.
t.abra pampa@-22.7,-65.7:

t.syktyvkar@61.6,50.8:
Syktyvkar is the capital of the Komi Republic, and it feels like a capital of a very large, very empty country. Autumn is short and golden, and winter is long, dark and very cold. If you can, aim for June to September.

The city has all you need: petrol stations all around, shops, cafés serving soup, dumplings and fish, and hotels of all kinds. It is the best place to stock up before heading further north or east, because services thin out quickly. Check your tyres, carry water, and keep your fuel topped up.

Take a walk along the river in the evening, when the light is soft. It is a calm place at the edge of the great northern forest.
t.socaire@-23.6,-67.9:
Socaire is a small oasis village in the Atacama Desert, standing at about 3,200 metres above sea level on the road from San Pedro de Atacama to the high plateau. Bring water, warm clothing, a hat and sunscreen, since the sun at this altitude is fierce and nights are cold.

The surrounding landscape is austere and magnificent. Reddish hills, pale salt flats, dark lava fields and the cones of the volcanoes make a palette that changes with the light, and the silence is deep. Vicuñas graze on the high slopes, and at dawn you may see flamingos on the nearby lagoons. The altitude demands respect, so drink plenty, move slowly, and sleep low if you feel unwell. t.miscanti lagoons@-23.7,-67.8:
Laguna Miscanti and its smaller neighbour Laguna Miñiques lie at about 4,100 metres in the Chilean Altiplano, among the high volcanoes of the Atacama, and they are some of the most beautiful lakes in northern Chile. The lakes are part of the Los Flamencos National Reserve, and their position, high on the plateau with nothing between them and the sky, gives them a stark, strange beauty that is hard to forget.

The gradient is gentle, but the altitude is the real challenge, and the thin air saps the power of a motorcycle and the energy of a rider. Mornings are clear and cold, with frost on the ground, while afternoons bring wind that can whip up dust and chill the lake into ripples. In summer, from December to March, afternoon storms can bring brief rain and even hail to the high ground.

The lagoons are a haven for wildlife. Flamingos feed in the shallows, vicuñas graze on the grassy slopes, and the Andean fox hunts across the plain. You may also see the large, fast-running rhea-like bird known as the suri, and if you are lucky, a flash of Andean gull or a duck. The silence is broken only by wind and the occasional cry of a bird. Breathe slowly, take a few pictures and then sit for a while. At this height and in this light, the world feels very clean.
t.tupiza@-21.4,-65.7:
The first thing that strikes you about Tupiza is the colour. Tupiza is the nearest town to the area where, according to the story most often told, the outlaws Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid met their end in 1908, after robbing a mine payroll in the district. The tale has been told in local shops and guesthouses ever since.

The landscape is the main reason to be here. Short rides take you out of town into the Quebrada de Palala, the Valle de los Machos with its odd columns of rock, and the Puerta del Diablo, a rock arch, with roads that follow dry riverbeds, climb rocky ridges and switch from tarmac to gravel in a few hundred metres. Cacti stand on the slopes, the sky is nearly always clear, and the red walls glow at sunrise and dusk, which is when to ride. At midday the sun is strong and the shadows disappear.

Tupiza is also a handy waypoint. It lies on the north-south road between Potosí and the Argentine frontier at Villazón, and further east the road drops toward lower valleys. The town itself is a lively, low-rise place of more than twenty thousand people, with a plaza, a market, and a small collection of guesthouses used to overlanders. You will find fuel, food and basic repairs here without difficulty, which is worth knowing because the next stretches are long.

Eat at the market for hearty plates of rice, meat and potato, and ask in town about local guides if you want to go deep into the canyons on horseback, an excellent alternative on a day when the bike needs rest. Winters are dry, bright and cold at night, while the summer rains can make gravel tracks slick, so plan your riding for the dry months and keep an eye on the sky. Dust is part of the deal, so protect your air filter and carry water.
t.villazon@-22.1,-65.6:
Villazón is where Bolivia ends, and it is the sort of border town that lives off crossing and trade. From Tupiza, you ride south along a high valley with red hills falling away on either side, with the road climbing gently over the open plateau and passing herds of llamas and the occasional adobe village. The Argentine side opens onto Ruta 9, the road that runs south toward Humahuaca and Jujuy through the Quebrada de Humahuaca, one of the great valleys of the continent, with its painted hills, so crossing here sets up a superb ride. Behind you, Bolivia's long highland road is coming to its end.

For practical needs, Villazón is a real town of around thirty thousand people, so there is fuel, food and cash machines, but prices and rules for foreign-plated vehicles at the pumps can differ, and in Argentina fuel can be cheaper or dearer depending on the year, so ask and plan accordingly. The small restaurants near the market serve filling soups and grilled meat that are exactly right for the cold. Change leftover bolivianos before crossing, as they are hard to use elsewhere, and top up your tank on the Argentine side if you have the chance.
t.segment catarpe norte@-22.8,-68.2:
North of San Pedro de Atacama, the San Pedro river has cut a narrow valley through the red and ochre hills of the Cordillera de la Sal, and along its edge runs a section of the Qhapaq Ñan, the great road network of the Inca Empire. The tracks into the Catarpe valley are dirt and gravel, sometimes sandy, sometimes rocky, with river crossings that can be tricky after rare summer rains. The views are extraordinary: eroded cliffs, salt-crusted ridges and the snow-capped cone of Licancabur volcano on the horizon. Afternoon winds can be strong, and the temperature swings from hot days to freezing nights. Carry plenty of water and protect yourself from the intense sun.

The Atacama has been inhabited for thousands of years, and the Atacameño people, or Lickanantay, built fortified villages, irrigated fields and traded across the Andes long before the Inca arrived. The Pukará de Quitor, a stone fortress near San Pedro, was the scene of a fierce battle with Spanish conquistadors in 1540. The Inca road connected this oasis to the wider empire, and remnants of walls, paths and structures can still be seen along the valley.

The landscape is stark but beautiful. The river supports a thin green ribbon of vegetation, including chañar and algarrobo trees, and you might see vicuñas, foxes or flamingos in the wider area. At sunset, the hills glow red and purple, and the night sky is among the clearest in the world, which is why major observatories are located nearby.

San Pedro de Atacama, about nine kilometres away, has fuel, food and accommodation, though supplies can be expensive and the fuel station sometimes has queues. Calama, about a hundred kilometres away, is the nearest large town. Plan your fuel carefully, as distances between stations in the Atacama are long, and respect local rules about access to archaeological and indigenous sites.
t.parc national de masoala@-15.2,50.3:
Masoala is the biggest national park in Madagascar, a huge peninsula of rainforest, mangrove and coral reef in the north-east of the island, and it is listed by UNESCO as part of the Rainforests of the Atsinanana, a group of eastern reserves that hold some of the richest wildlife on earth. Red ruffed lemurs, found nowhere else, move high in the canopy, and the aye-aye, the strange nocturnal lemur with long fingers, lives in the trees. The park meets the sea in a coastline of white beaches, rocky headlands and fringing reef, and in winter humpback whales come to calve in the Bay of Antongil to the west. Much of the land beyond the coastal fringe is only reached by boat or on foot, so Masoala is not a place for riding a motorbike inside the park. The ride here is to the edge of the forest, and the adventure belongs to the trails.

Antalaha, a port town of about thirty-four thousand people, is the capital of the vanilla coast. The vanilla orchid was brought to Madagascar from Mexico, and its pods are cured by hand in the sun, a long process that makes the sweet smell of the air around the town in the season. The surrounding area produces a large share of the world's vanilla, and the economy rises and falls with its price, as does the safety of the crop, which is sometimes guarded by farmers against thieves.

The dry season, roughly from September to December, is the best time, though rain can fall at any moment. A rider here should be self-sufficient, with spare parts, a good tool kit and patience. Fuel is available in Antalaha but is not reliable outside the larger towns, so fill up whenever possible. Local meals are simple: rice, fish and zebu meat with tomato and chilli sauce, often served with fresh tropical fruit.
t.karaman ata@43.9,51.9:
Mangystau is the bleak, brilliant desert peninsula on the eastern shore of the Caspian Sea, in the far west of Kazakhstan. It looks like the surface of another planet, with chalk cliffs, canyons, salt flats, strange rock formations and fossil seabeds from the days when this was an ocean. For centuries it has also been a land of Sufi pilgrimage, and its network of underground mosques, cut into the soft limestone, is the reason for the UNESCO listing that includes this site. Karaman-Ata is one of the sacred sites that mark the memory of a holy man, in a quiet spot among low cliffs, reached by a path and accompanied by a small cemetery and shrine.

The underground mosques of the region, such as Beket-Ata and Shopan-Ata, were built by nomadic people who needed shelter from the heat and wind. Visitors should dress modestly and leave their shoes at the door, and keep voices low.

Take water, at least several litres, and a spare tyre. Locals are hospitable, and tea with bread, dried fruit and sometimes camel milk is the usual welcome. The sites are best visited with a guide, who knows the tracks and the etiquette.
t.segment incahuasi norte@-22.1,-68.6:
The Inca built a road system, the Qhapaq Ñan, that ran for tens of thousands of kilometres through six modern countries, from Colombia to Chile and Argentina, and parts of it climb into the driest desert in the world.
