I cannot say precisely what the Incahuasi stretch looks like, and I would be inventing detail if I tried. The region itself I can describe. This is a landscape of ochre plains, black lava, white salt crusts and cone volcanoes, at heights above three thousand metres, with a blue sky and a dry cold wind that can scour exposed skin. The air is thin, the nights are bitter, and the silence is complete. Guanacos and vicuñas graze in the tussock grass, and flamingos feed in the saline lagoons.

Riding here is high-desert adventure. Main roads such as the one from Calama to San Pedro are paved and good, but the tracks toward archaeological sites are gravel, sand and washboard, and side roads can be washed out after rare rains. Altitude affects both rider and engine, and fuel consumption rises, so plan more range than you think. Winter nights fall well below freezing, and there is a short summer rain season, called the Altiplanic winter, that can bring flooding.

No town is listed close to this point, so treat it as remote. San Pedro de Atacama has fuel, restaurants and lodging, and Calama is the larger city for repairs and supplies. Carry extra fuel, water, warm clothing and a tyre kit, and tell someone your route. Respect archaeological remains, never move stones, and keep to existing tracks, since the desert surface holds a scar for decades. Sun protection is vital at this altitude.
t.segment santa rosa de tastil@-24.4,-65.9:
The Quebrada del Toro is a long, narrow valley cut through the Andes of Salta, in north-west Argentina, and the old road that follows it was a trade route for centuries. Santa Rosa de Tastil sits on a terrace above the river, at around 3,200 metres, and it was a town: a settlement of stone houses, perhaps several hundred of them, built in the fourteenth century and inhabited until shortly before the Spanish conquest. People here farmed, kept llamas and traded across the mountains, and when the Incas arrived they connected the place to their road system, the Qhapaq Nan, which was inscribed by UNESCO in 2014.

Walking through the ruins is oddly moving. The foundations of rectangular houses, packed close together and stepped up the hillside, make a pattern you can read at a glance, and the surrounding hills are a deep red and brown, dotted with tall cardon cacti. A small museum beside the site shows pottery, textiles and tools found here, and a local guide can explain how the town worked. The air is dry and thin, the sun is hard, and the wind picks up in the afternoon.

The ride up the Quebrada del Toro on Ruta 51 from Salta is one of the finest in the north of Argentina. The road follows the river, crosses it several times, and climbs through gorges of coloured rock toward the high plateau of the Puna, with the railway that carries the Tren a las Nubes visible above you in places. The tarmac is generally good, with some patchy sections, and the curves are long and open. Above Tastil, the road climbs to the pass of Abra Blanca, over four thousand metres, and the cold and thin air are noticeable.

Fuel is not available in the village. Fill up in Salta before the climb, and again in San Antonio de los Cobres, farther up the road, and carry a reserve. Altitude can cause headaches and tiredness, so take it slowly. Weather is dry for most of the year, with summer storms from December to March. Mornings are best for light and wind.
t.segment cupo topain@-22.1,-68.3:
In the far north of Chile, the Atacama Desert holds some of the driest ground on Earth, and the Loa river is the only stream that crosses it, carving a green line through the sand and rock. The road between Cupo and Topain follows a stretch of the Inca trail through this country, high in the Andean foothills above Calama and San Pedro de Atacama, a segment of the Qhapaq Nan, the Inca road network inscribed by UNESCO in 2014.

Along these old routes, llama caravans carried salt, copper and food between the coast, the desert oases and the high plateau, and the Incas built tambos, resting places with storehouses, along the way. The landscape is vast and empty, with mineral-coloured hills, volcanoes on the horizon, and villages of adobe houses with small churches and terraced fields. The people here are Atacameno, or Likan Antay, and their culture combines ancient traditions with Catholic festivals.

The desert is a place of extremes. Days are hot and bright, nights are bitterly cold, and the air is so dry that the stars seem close enough to touch. At altitudes above three thousand metres, the sun is strong and the air thin. Rain is almost unknown, but in the summer, storms from the Altiplano can send flash floods down dry gullies. The best time to ride is from March to November, with clear skies.

Nothing at these coordinates carries a name I can vouch for, so think of this as a stop in the high country of the Loa valley, away from any town. Roads in this area vary from good tarmac to rough gravel, and distances are long. Fuel is the main concern: fill up in Calama or San Pedro de Atacama, both with several stations, and carry a spare can, since there will be none out here. Bring water, food, warm clothing, and let someone know your route. Mobile coverage is patchy.
t.humahuaca@-23.2,-65.3:
Humahuaca sits at almost three thousand metres in the Quebrada de Humahuaca, a long, dry, colourful valley in the far north of Argentina that UNESCO has listed as a World Heritage landscape. The valley runs for about a hundred and fifty kilometres, with the river Grande flowing between walls of red, ochre, green and violet rock, and cardón cacti standing like candelabra on the hillsides. The road through it, the Ruta 9, follows an ancient trade route used by the Incas, and before them by many peoples who carried llama caravans between the Andes and the lowlands.

The town is small and adobe-built, with narrow cobbled streets and a lively market, where women sell woven goods, dried herbs, coca leaves and local food. In the main square, a clock tower on the old town hall has a figure of Saint Francis Solano that emerges at noon to bless the crowd, a daily show that draws tourists. A large stone monument to the heroes of independence stands on a hill above the town, reached by a steep staircase, and its view over the rooftops and the valley is a good reward for the climb.

The altitude is a real factor. Mountain sickness can strike newcomers, and locals recommend drinking tea made from coca leaves and taking it easy for the first day. Food here is simple and hearty, with llama stew, tamales, humitas made from corn and quinoa in many forms, and strong flavours from the aji pepper. Carnival, in February, is a wild celebration with flour, water and costumed dancers, mixing Catholic and indigenous traditions.

On a motorbike, the valley is a joy, with wide bends, long views and mostly good surfaces. Wind and dust are frequent, the sun is intense at this altitude, and temperatures swing from freezing at night to warm by day. Fuel is available in Humahuaca, and you should fill up there, since distances to the next stations can be long. Nearby, the painted hills of Purmamarca and Hornocal show the colours of the valley at their best.
t.laguna colorada@-22.2,-67.8:
Laguna Colorada lies at about 4,300 metres on the Bolivian Altiplano, inside the Eduardo Avaroa Andean Fauna National Reserve, and it is one of the strangest sights in South America. The water is a deep rust red, stained by algae and sediments, and it is dotted with white islands of borax and salt, with thousands of flamingos wading in the shallows. Three species, the Andean, the Chilean and James's flamingo, feed here, and the contrast of pink birds, red water and white crust against a backdrop of brown volcanic peaks is almost too much.

The altitude is the main fact of life. The air carries less than two thirds of the oxygen at sea level, engines lose power and riders feel it, with headaches, breathlessness and slow thinking. Acclimatise for several days in Uyuni or at similar heights before coming, drink water, avoid alcohol and be ready to turn back. Nights are bitterly cold, often well below freezing, and the wind is strong and constant, so dress for winter even in summer.

The route here from Uyuni is a track of sand, gravel and corrugated ripio, crossing salt flats and open desert, and it is a serious undertaking on two wheels. Road bikes will struggle, and even adventure bikes need skill, as soft sand and washboard surfaces are tiring, and river crossings can be deep. Many travellers go by four-wheel drive with a driver, and riders should be self-sufficient, with spare fuel, water, tools and a satellite communicator.

The reserve charges an entry fee, payable in cash, and the basic refugios, simple hostels with shared rooms and bare food, are the main accommodation. A few kilometres on lie the Sol de Mañana geyser field, a steaming landscape of boiling mud at nearly five thousand metres, and the Laguna Verde, a green lake beneath the Licancabur volcano on the Chilean border.

Come in the dry season, from roughly May to October, when roads are firm. The silence, the colour and the flamingos at sunrise, with the lake blushing in the early light, are the memory you take away.
t.paso de jama@-23.2,-67.0:
Nothing prepares you for the quiet at Paso de Jama. At about 4,200 metres, the border between Argentina and Chile lies on the Altiplano, a huge, high plateau of tawny grass, salt flats and shallow lakes, ringed by volcanoes. The sky is a hard, deep blue, the air is thin and dry, and the only sounds are the wind and the occasional passing truck. Flamingos feed in the pale lagoons, and vicuñas, the delicate wild cousins of the llama, graze beside the road.

The road is the main route between Salta and Jujuy and the Atacama desert, and the ride here is a high-altitude marathon. On the Argentine side, Route 52 climbs from the Salinas Grandes salt flat and the Cuesta de Lipán, a mountain road with dozens of hairpins, to the plateau, and then runs straight and fast across it, before dropping steeply on the Chilean side to San Pedro de Atacama, more than a thousand metres lower. The tarmac is generally good, but wind, ice and snow can close the road at short notice.

Altitude is the real challenge. Sickness can hit anyone, and a bike with a carburettor or an old fuel-injection system may run rough in the thin air, so be prepared. Drink water, move slowly and do not overdo it. The temperature can drop below freezing at night in any month, and the wind is strong and cold in the afternoon. Warm gloves and a windproof layer are essential.

The nearest stations are at Susques on the Argentine side and at San Pedro de Atacama in Chile, roughly three hundred kilometres apart, so fill the tank and carry extra. The border posts have opening hours and paperwork, including vehicle permits, and the process can be long. Do not rush it. Take a hot drink, enjoy the silence and the huge landscape, and plan to arrive in San Pedro by evening, where the nights are cool and the stars are astonishing.
t.sol de manana@-22.4,-67.8:
Sol de Mañana is a field of steaming holes in the ground at nearly five thousand metres, on the high desert of south-west Bolivia, and arriving there feels like landing on a small, hostile planet. Fumaroles hiss from the cracked, yellow-stained earth, mud pots bubble and plop, and a smell of sulphur hangs in the cold air. At dawn, when the temperature is below freezing and the steam is at its thickest, the whole field looks as if it were on fire, and the sun comes up behind it in ribbons of orange.

The geothermal field lies in the Eduardo Avaroa National Reserve, a vast area of salt lakes, volcanoes and desert on the Bolivian altiplano close to the Chilean border. This is some of the most remote country in South America, with flamingos on Laguna Colorada, a lake stained red by algae and minerals, and, further south, the green and white shores of Laguna Verde under the cone of Licancabur. The reserve charges an entrance fee, and the tracks are mostly unsurfaced, sandy or gravelled and often corrugated, with soft patches that can swallow a loaded motorcycle.

Riding here is serious expedition travel. The distances between services are huge, the altitude is brutal, and there is almost no help if something goes wrong. Altitude sickness is a danger and breathing is hard, so take time to acclimatise in Uyuni or elsewhere first. Engines run poorly in thin air, nights are bitterly cold, and the wind arrives in the afternoon, driving sand across the plain. Many riders go with a support vehicle or with a local guide, which is sensible, and most visitors arrive by jeep from Uyuni on a three-day trip that crosses the salt flat.

At the field itself, stay well away from the edges of the pools and the thin ground between them. The crust is fragile, the mud is hot enough to scald badly, and people have died by stepping where they should not. Stay on the paths, keep your distance from the steam vents, and do not let children wander. The ground can look solid and be a thin skin over boiling mud.

There are no services at the geysers. Carry extra fuel, water, food, warm clothing and tools, and tell someone your route. Shortly after dawn is the best time, when the steam is at its peak and the light is soft, and it is also the coldest, so bring gloves that you can really trust.
t.valle de la luna@-22.9,-68.3:
Ten kilometres from San Pedro de Atacama, the land turns into something that looks borrowed from another planet, which is how the Valle de la Luna got its name. The valley is part of the Cordillera de la Sal, a range of ridges formed by folded salt and clay that have been squeezed, cracked and eroded by wind into fins, gullies and crusted white ridges. The ground is pale and brittle, and in places the salt crystallises on the surface in a thin frost that crackles under your boots. This is the driest desert in the world, and every detail of it feels sharpened by that fact.

The best moment is the end of the day. Before sunset the ridges turn from beige to orange and then to pink, with the Licancabur volcano standing in the distance above the Bolivian border and the long shadows making the folds look three-dimensional. Crowds gather on the dune viewpoints for exactly this reason, so be ready to share the light, and bring a layer, because the temperature drops sharply once the sun slips behind the Domeyko range. At midday the glare is fierce and the air is bone dry, so water matters more than people think.

The riding around San Pedro is made of long straight paved roads, gravel tracks, and a lot of space. The road to the valley is short and manageable, but the surrounding area is full of sand, corrugations and wind that can push a bike off line on exposed stretches. Keep an eye on the weather and the surface, particularly if you head off the main road, and carry plenty of fluids. Altitude here is already about 2,400 metres, so give yourself a day to adjust before heading up to the lagoons.

San Pedro itself is a low adobe town of narrow streets, with a few thousand permanent residents and a steady flow of travellers, tour agencies and cafes. It has fuel, but it is worth filling the tank and carrying spare capacity if you plan a longer loop, because the distances out here are large and the next pump can be far. The village also has a small church dating back to the colonial era, and the Atacameño people who lived here long before the Spanish still shape its culture.

There is an entry charge for the protected area, and rules about staying on marked routes, which protect the fragile salt formations. Respect them and the valley will look the same for the next rider.
Two blue lagoons lie at about 4,200 metres on the altiplano south of San Pedro de Atacama, and they look unreal. Laguna Miscanti and its smaller neighbour Laguna Miñiques sit at the foot of the volcanoes of the same names, with Cerro Miscanti rising above 5,600 metres to the west, and the water is a hard, cold blue against the tawny grass and bare rock. Flamingos feed in the shallows, vicuñas graze nearby, and the wind combs the surface into ripples. It is a protected reserve, and the staff at the entrance keep an eye on how close visitors get to the shore.

The road to get here is the main attraction for many riders. From San Pedro you climb the long valley toward Socaire, passing through a landscape of dry riverbeds and ancient volcanic flows, and the altitude increases steadily. It is mostly paved, but the sections near the lagoons can be gravelly, and the temperature falls by many degrees as you gain height. The air is thin, and a bike can feel noticeably flat on the climbs, so treat the engine with some mercy. The wind is persistent and often strong, especially in the afternoon.

Altitude demands respect. A lot of travellers arrive from sea level and push straight up to over four thousand metres, which is a recipe for headaches, nausea and poor judgement. Spend a couple of days in San Pedro first, drink plenty of water, and ride slowly. Sun protection matters, because at this height the ultraviolet radiation is intense even on a cold day, and a cheerful bright morning can burn your face before you notice.

Fill the tank, carry a spare can if you can, and take food and water. Socaire, a small farming village along the route, has terraced fields watered by ancient channels and a little church worth a glance, but services are basic. In winter, snow and ice can close sections or make them treacherous, so check conditions before you leave town.

Come in the morning, when the water is calmer and the light on the volcanoes is crisp. By afternoon the wind has a mind of its own.
t.salar de talar@-23.9,-67.6:
Past the lagoons the road keeps climbing into country that has no obvious owner. The Salar de Talar lies on the high Atacama plateau, a flat white pan at well over four thousand metres, ringed by pale volcanic cones and washed with a thin skin of brine. It is part of the vast chain of salt flats that fills the basins between the Andes and the Domeyko range, each one formed when a lake dried up and left its minerals behind. The result is a landscape of extraordinary simplicity: salt, sky and the occasional cloud shadow moving across the plain.

For a rider, this is remote riding in the real sense. The route toward Paso Sico, the high border crossing to Argentina, leads across open terrain with few buildings, very little traffic and long gravel stretches. The surface can be hard-packed and fast, then suddenly sandy or corrugated, and the wind builds through the day. The scale fools your eye, so distances that look short can take much longer than you expect. Keep your speed under control, and keep an eye on the ground for soft patches near the salt flat edges.

The wildlife is sparse but striking. Flamingos gather in shallow lagoons on the salar margins, vicuñas pick their way across the scrub, and now and then a fox slinks off. The sky is intensely clear at night, which is why this region is home to some of the world's major observatories, and if you are camping or staying in a nearby village, the stars are dazzling beyond belief. It is also cold: night temperatures drop well below freezing, even in summer.

Practical issues are serious here. San Pedro de Atacama, a good hundred kilometres or more away, is the only reliable place to refuel, and Socaire has very basic supplies at best. Ride with a full tank, spare fuel, food and water, a basic tool kit and a satellite messenger if you have one, and tell someone where you are going. The border crossing has its own opening hours and conditions, and weather can close it.

Altitude sickness is a real risk above four thousand metres, so give yourself time to adapt and do not push your pace. The reward is solitude, light and a feeling of scale you rarely get elsewhere.
t.parc national de masoala@-15.6,50.2:
Madagascar's north-east corner is a great green thumb pushed into the Indian Ocean, and the Masoala peninsula is the wildest part of it. The national park covers a vast area of lowland rainforest, mangroves, and coast, and it holds the largest protected tract of the island's eastern rainforest, which is why it is bundled into the Rainforests of the Atsinanana World Heritage listing. Behind the beaches, the forest runs up steep hills in layer after layer of palms, vines, orchids and giant trees.

I have to be straight with the rider here: there is no road riding in Masoala itself. The peninsula has essentially no road network, and the usual gateway is the small town of Maroantsetra, on the bay of Antongil to the north-west, reached by small plane or by long, rough overland journeys on tracks that turn to mud in the rains. From there, boats carry visitors along the coast or across the bay. Any motorcycle story in this region is one of rough tracks, river crossings by pirogue, and plenty of time. The drier months, roughly September to December, are the most forgiving, while the cyclone season from January to March can cut access altogether.

What the place gives in exchange is a sense of living nature. Masoala is home to the red ruffed lemur, found only on this peninsula, whose loud, rolling calls carry through the canopy at dawn. There are also aye-ayes, fossas, chameleons ranging from tiny leaf species to the big panther chameleon, and a startling variety of frogs, geckos and birds. Humpback whales pass through the bay between July and September, coming to breed and calve. The forest smells of wet earth and leaf, and the sound at night is a chorus of frogs and insects.

Practical matters are few, and they are firm. Bring waterproofs, insect repellent, sturdy boots, and cash in Malagasy ariary, since cards are rarely accepted. The people along this coast are mostly Betsimisaraka, and their villages of palm-thatch and plank houses are friendly places, where a polite greeting goes a long way.
t.rock mosques and associated sacred sites:
The Mangystau peninsula in western Kazakhstan looks like the surface of another planet: chalk cliffs, red canyons, salt flats, and a plateau, the Ustyurt, that stretches away to a horizon without a tree. In this empty land, where the Caspian Sea lies far to the west and the nearest big town is Aktau on the coast, a number of holy sites are cut into the soft limestone, the so-called rock mosques. These are underground or cave-like sanctuaries, some hollowed out centuries ago, associated with Sufi teachers and with the ancestors of the local Kazakh clans.

Getting here is a long, spacious drive. The roads between the settlements are straight and fast where they are good and cratered where they are not, so it is important to read the surface well ahead. Wind is a constant, the sky is enormous, and the temperature swings from fierce summer heat, over forty degrees, to a bitter winter. Spring and autumn are best, when the colours of the land, ochre, white and rose, are at their softest. Camels wander across the road, and a stray herd can appear at the crest of a hill, so ride within your sight distance.

The shrines connect with a caravan history. Trade routes crossed this peninsula between the Caspian ports and the cities of Khiva and Bukhara, and pilgrims who walked the long way across the Ustyurt found shelter and prayer at these places. Names such as Beket-Ata, the Sufi teacher of the eighteenth century whose underground mosque is the most visited, run through the region, and local people still make pilgrimages, often in family groups, sleeping at simple guesthouses and eating in shared halls. Visitors should dress modestly, remove their shoes where asked, and treat the sites with respect, since these are live places of devotion, not theme parks.

For fuel, the nearest town of consequence is Shetpe, with about twelve thousand people, roughly twenty kilometres from the coordinates. Fill up there, take far more water than you think you need, and carry food. Mobile signal fades in the open desert. Tell someone where you are going, and avoid riding in the dark, when the combination of potholes, animals and distance turns small mistakes into long problems.
t.shakpak ata@44.4,51.1:
Shakpak-Ata is another of the holy places of the Mangystau region, a desert shrine in the northern part of the peninsula, where the rocky Ustyurt plateau drops into canyons and dry valleys of white and orange stone. The name refers to a revered figure, Shakpak, who is said to have been a Sufi saint of the area, and the complex is built into the slope of a ravine, with prayer rooms, an underground mosque and a necropolis of carved gravestones, some of them marked with symbols of horses and weapons that tell of the clan's history.

The ride here is an exercise in distance and silence. Taūshyq, a village of a couple of thousand people about twenty kilometres away, is the closest settlement. On the final stretch, the road may shrink to gravel or desert track, with wheel ruts, patches of soft sand and the occasional steep dry wash, so a bike with decent ground clearance and a rider with experience will be happier than a heavy tourer. Wind is routine, heat is intense in summer, and the nights can freeze in winter. The light, especially in the evening, turns the cliffs a deep rose.

Pilgrims come here from all over Kazakhstan, and the tradition of walking, sleeping at the shrine and praying is an old one. You will often meet families sharing food and tea in simple guesthouses or in the open air, and a stranger who arrives politely is usually welcomed. Dress conservatively, take off your shoes where others do, and ask before taking photographs, particularly of worshippers. The silence in the shrine's cool rooms is remarkable after the glare outside.

Fuel and supplies are the crux. The nearest town with any reliable service is Shetpe, farther along the main road, and even that will not be near. Fill every tank and container you can, and carry more water than you expect to drink, plus food, spare tubes and a basic repair kit. Telephone coverage drops away in the gullies. Check that you have permissions for the border zone in the region, because some parts of western Kazakhstan are controlled, and tell someone back in town where you are heading and when you plan to return.
t.san salvador de jujuy@-24.2,-65.3:
Jujuy, as everyone calls it, sits in a green bowl about 1,200 metres up in the far north-west of Argentina, where the wet forests of the eastern slope meet the dry high country behind. The city was founded in 1593, on the third attempt, after earlier settlements were wiped out or abandoned, and it still has the look of a provincial capital that has had to work for its place. About three hundred thousand people live here, with the river Xibi Xibi running through the middle of town and the hills of the Yungas closing in on three sides. It is the usual start for the long climb into the Andes.

The history you notice is political. In 1812 General Belgrano ordered the whole population to leave the city and burn what they could not carry, so the royalist army would find nothing, a sacrifice remembered every August as the Éxodo Jujeño. Today the main square, with its cathedral and its gilded pulpit, is a relaxed place of shoeshine stalls and old men reading the paper, and the market is worth a wander for coca leaves, cheese, spices and woven goods.

For a rider, Jujuy is the gateway to two of the great roads of the continent. Ruta 9 heads north up the Quebrada de Humahuaca, the painted valley that earned a UNESCO listing in 2003, with its striped hills, adobe villages and cactus forests. Ruta 52, branching west through Purmamarca, climbs over the Cuesta de Lipán, passing 4,000 metres before dropping to the white salt flats and on towards Paso de Jama and Chile. The first kilometres out of town are fast, then the valley narrows, the vegetation thins, and the colours begin to change from green to ochre to red.

This is where to be sensible. Altitude arrives faster than you think, and so does cold: even in summer, the high stretches can be near freezing at dawn, with afternoon storms from December to March that bring rockfalls and washouts on the quebrada roads. Fill the tank here, or at the stations in Palpalá and the larger towns, because fuel out on the high road is sparse and sometimes rationed or simply unavailable in small villages. Drink water, chew coca if the locals swear by it, and take things slowly on day one. Eat humitas or an empanada salteña and a cold beer in the plaza before you set off, then go to bed early. The mountains reward those who start early and stop often.
t.parc national de masoala@-15.8,50.0:
Masoala is the largest national park in Madagascar, covering more than two thousand square kilometers of rainforest on a rugged peninsula in the northeast, and this point lies on its western side, facing Antongil Bay. The bay is wide, deep and sheltered, one of the best places in the Indian Ocean to see humpback whales, which come to calve between about July and September. The town of Maroantsetra, at the head of the bay, is the usual gateway, a quiet, humid place with a river, a market and boats waiting at the shore.

The forest here is among the richest in the country. Masoala is the only home of the red ruffed lemur, a large and noisy animal whose chorus can carry across the valley, and it shelters aye-ayes, fossas, dozens of chameleon species, tiny leaf-tailed geckos and a huge variety of orchids and palms. Rain falls through much of the year, up to several meters, so the leaf litter is thick and the air carries the smell of wet earth. Together with other eastern rainforests, the park is part of the UNESCO site called the Rainforests of the Atsinanana, listed in 2007.

For anyone thinking of riding, the truth is that there are few roads here. The peninsula has no through route, and the park is reached mostly by boat across the bay or by trails on foot. The roads that do exist around Maroantsetra are dirt and mud, often impassable in the cyclone season from January to March, and suited to local motorbikes and sturdy four-wheel-drive vehicles. Even in the dry months, from about September to November, streams must be crossed and ferries waited for.

Services are limited. Maroantsetra has a few small guesthouses, and fuel is limited and sold in small quantities, so plan on carrying what you need if you come by road. Trips into the park are best arranged with local guides who can arrange boats, camping and permits.

If you stay on the water, the evening is memorable. Fishermen paddle out in dugout canoes with the forest dark behind them, and the call of a lemur floats across the bay as the light fades.
t.parc national de masoala@-15.6,50.1:
Deeper into the Masoala peninsula, away from the bay, the land climbs into steep ridges covered in wet forest, and here the sense of remoteness grows. The park has no real roads through this interior, and rivers and footpaths are the arteries. Heavy rain, which can exceed five or six meters a year, feeds streams that rush down the slopes, and the forest is thick with tree ferns, climbing bamboo and epiphytes. It is a hot, humid world where leaves drip all night and the ground is covered in moss.

The wildlife is shy and hidden, and patience is rewarded. Chameleons, including the tiny leaf chameleons, sit on twigs at night where a flashlight picks them out, and the spectacular Parson's and panther chameleons are found in the lower forest. The tailless tenrec, mouse lemurs and the elusive aye-aye live in the canopy, and at night you may hear the high, cat-like calls of the red ruffed lemur. Birds such as the helmet vanga and the Madagascar serpent eagle are rare sights, and the forest is rich in orchids.

Local people live on the edges, practicing small-scale agriculture and fishing, and many work as guides. The Betsimisaraka communities have a close relationship with the forest, and traditional taboos, called fady, protect certain places and species. Respect for those customs is part of visiting, and guides will explain what is allowed. As for riding, the truth is that this area is not for motorcycles. The nearest roads are rough tracks around Maroantsetra and the villages of the coast, and even four-wheel-drive vehicles struggle during the wet season. Cyclones can hit between January and March, when travel is difficult or impossible. The drier months from September to December are the best time to visit, though showers can occur at any time. Most visitors arrive by boat and hike with a guide. Bring what you need, including water purification, rain gear and plenty of insect repellent. Camping and simple lodges provide a place to sleep, and food is basic, with rice, beans and fish.

The reward is a sense of wildness that few places can match. At night, the forest hums with life, and the stars above the clearing seem close enough to touch.
t.parc national de masoala@-15.3,50.3:
At the northern tip of the Masoala peninsula, the land swings toward Cap Est, the eastern point of Madagascar, and the landscape changes. The rainforest here meets the Indian Ocean directly, with white beaches, coral reefs and rocky headlands, and in places the trees reach almost to the waterline. This is the exposed side of Masoala, battered by cyclones and strong swells, and it is a wilder coast than the sheltered bay on the west.

The marine parks that belong to Masoala protect reefs and islands offshore, where turtles, dolphins and, from July to September, humpback whales pass close to the shore. Snorkeling is possible in calm conditions, and the coral in places is healthy. On land, the forest holds the same species found elsewhere in the park, with lemurs, chameleons and many birds, but visitors often notice the sea first, with its sound and smell present in every part of the forest.

The towns to the north, Antalaha and Sambava, are the centers of Madagascar's vanilla industry. The coast here is lined with vanilla vines trained on trees and poles, and the beans are pollinated by hand, a delicate and labor-intensive job. In the harvest season, the smell of curing vanilla fills the air around the villages. The industry has made this region richer than many parts of Madagascar, but prices swing wildly and thefts are common.

The roads in the area are rough. The coastal route between Antalaha and the peninsula is dirt and mud, often washed out by rain, and in cyclone season from January to March, it can be impassable. Smaller local motorbikes are the usual transport, and a sturdy dual-sport machine with a skilled rider can manage in dry weather. Streams are crossed by fords and ferries, and there is no official road around the peninsula. Local guidance is almost essential. Fuel is available in Antalaha and Sambava, but not in the villages, and supplies can be limited, so carry extra. Food is simple, with rice, fish and tropical fruit, and accommodation ranges from small guesthouses in town to basic huts on the coast. The best months are September to December, when the rain eases and the sea is calmer. In the evening, with the surf rolling in and the forest darkening behind, the place feels like the edge of the world.
t.san juan bolivia@-21.3,-67.7:
San Juan is a speck on the high, dry southwestern edge of Bolivia, where the Altiplano turns into a landscape of salt, volcanic rock and sky. It lies south of Uyuni, on the route that heads toward Laguna Colorada and the Chilean border, and there is no larger town anywhere nearby, only a handful of houses, a few simple lodgings, some llama pens and miles of empty plateau. The height is well over 3,600 metres, so the air is thin, cold and very clear.

The riding here is expedition riding, not touring. The roads are mostly gravel, sand and corrugated tracks, with wash-outs, soft patches and crossings of dry streambeds, and they are often unmarked, so a GPS track and a companion are wise. Strong wind blows almost daily in the afternoon, raising dust and making progress slow. The nights are bitter, with temperatures well below freezing even in the dry season, and the middle of the day can be warm in the sun. The best time is the dry season, roughly May to October, but the cold is serious, and the rainy season, from December to March, can flood the salt and cut the tracks.

Fuel is a real planning issue. There are no reliable fuel stations out here, and riders carry spare fuel from Uyuni, where supplies and mechanics are found. Bring water, food, tools and a satellite messenger if you have one, because mobile coverage is absent and help is hours away. Tour operators run jeeps along these tracks, so you may meet them at lodgings, and they are a useful source of news about conditions.

The surroundings are astonishing. Volcanoes rise above the plateau, some of them steaming, with colours of rust, ochre and purple in the bare rock, while salt flats glimmer white in the distance. Vicunas, the wild relatives of the llama, graze in small groups, and flamingos feed in the lagoons farther south, their pink feathers brilliant against the grey-blue water. The air smells of dust and cold stone, and at night the stars are almost too many.

The people here are Quechua and Aymara herders and miners, and life is hard. Quinoa grows on the high plain, and llama meat is the main fare. Be polite, ask before taking photographs and carry small change for purchases.
t.laguna verde@-22.8,-67.8:
Laguna Verde is a colour you do not expect to find at four thousand three hundred metres, in a dry, wind-scoured corner of southwest Bolivia, a few kilometres from the Chilean border. The lake lies at the foot of Licancabur, a near-perfect volcanic cone that rises to about 5,900 metres on the frontier, and on a calm morning the cone is reflected in the water. The colour, a milky turquoise that can turn to emerald, comes from dissolved minerals, copper, magnesium, lead and arsenic among them, and it changes with the wind and the hour. Do not swim in it.

The surrounding country is the Eduardo Avaroa Andean Fauna National Reserve, a high desert of red and ochre rock, sand and sparse yellow grass. Nearby lagoons hold flamingos, and vicuñas pick their way across the slopes. A short drive away are the Sol de Mañana geysers, where boiling mud and steam hiss out of the ground in a landscape that smells of sulphur, and the Polques hot springs, where you can lie in warm water with the cold wind on your face. The Dalí Desert, with its odd scattered boulders, is another stop along the route.

For a motorcyclist this is serious country. The tracks are sand, gravel and washboard, with deep soft patches and loose rock, and you need a bike you can trust and the skills to match it. The altitude brings its own problems: the air is thin, engines lose power, and people can suffer from headaches and breathlessness, so give your body time to adjust and drink plenty of water. Wind builds in the afternoon, often fierce, and temperatures can drop well below freezing at night, even in summer. Dress as if you were riding in the Arctic, then add another layer.

Carry spare fuel, food, water, a repair kit and a means of calling for help, and ride with at least one other bike if possible. Entry to the reserve requires a fee, paid at a gate, and a basic refuge near the lagoon offers beds and meals. Come early, before the wind, and you will see the lake at its best.
t.paso sico@-23.8,-67.3:
Paso Sico is a border crossing between Argentina and Chile that lies at over 4,000 metres in the middle of the Altiplano, and it is more of an idea than a place. There are no villages, no shops, only a gravel road crossing a high, dry, wind-blasted plateau, with salt flats, volcanoes and small lakes that flash silver or pink in the sun. The route runs from the Argentine province of Salta to San Pedro de Atacama, in Chile, crossing a landscape that most people never see, and the sense of emptiness is overwhelming.

The scenery is immense. Salt pans lie in pale, flat expanses, with flamingos in shallow pools and vicuñas pacing across the dry grass. Volcanoes rise on all sides, many of them over five thousand metres, among them Socompa, on the border, whose eruption long ago left a vast landslide field. On the Chilean side, the road passes lakes such as Miscanti and Miñiques, which are a deep blue, set against reddish mountains, and the contrast is spectacular. The air is clear and thin, and the stars at night are astonishing.

This is not a road for the casual rider. The surface is mostly gravel and sand, with washboard, rocky patches and the occasional river crossing, and the weather can change sharply, with strong wind, snow and freezing temperatures even in summer. Altitude brings its own problems: engines lose power, and riders can suffer from headaches and fatigue, so acclimatise before you go. The border post may keep restricted hours or close in bad conditions, so check ahead and carry your paperwork. You must be self-reliant.

Fuel is the main practical issue. There are no pumps at the pass or anywhere near it, so carry enough fuel for the whole crossing and a margin, and plan your supplies in the nearest towns on each side. Calama, on the Chilean side, has large fuel stations and shops. Bring water, food and warm clothing, a repair kit, and a satellite communicator if you have one. Ride with at least one other vehicle and tell someone your route. If you do it right, you will remember the silence for years.
t.aktau@43.7,51.2:
Aktau is a city that grew out of the desert with the sea on one side and nothing on the other. Built in the Soviet era on the eastern shore of the Caspian, in the Mangystau region, it was first founded to support the mining of uranium and later oil, and for decades it was called Shevchenko, after the Ukrainian poet who had been exiled in the area. The name Aktau means white mountain, a reference to the pale chalk and limestone hills that rise behind. With roughly a hundred and fifty thousand people, it is the main port and regional hub.

A strange fact about Aktau: the city has almost no street names. Addresses are written by microdistrict number, building and apartment, a legacy of Soviet planning that takes some getting used to. Another is that there is almost no fresh water; for years a nuclear reactor on the coast powered a desalination plant, and the city still depends on treated seawater. The promenade along the Caspian is a pleasant place for an evening walk, and the sea, which is bluer than you might expect, is calm and warm in summer.

For a rider, Aktau is a base and a launch pad. The roads inland are long, straight and mostly paved, crossing a flat, dry landscape of clay, salt flats and scrub, with sudden canyons, chalk cliffs and strange rock formations. There is a lot of oil traffic, with big trucks, so overtake carefully, and wind can be strong enough to move a loaded bike across a lane. Distances are great and services scarce between settlements, so it pays to keep your tank full and your water bottles topped up.

Within the city, fuel, workshops, banks, supermarkets and hotels are plentiful. Seafood is limited because of the Caspian's conditions, but you will find good grilled fish, plenty of meat and Central Asian standards in the restaurants. A ferry connects the port with Baku in Azerbaijan, which is a point of interest for riders on longer trips, though schedules and rules need checking well ahead. In summer, expect heat above thirty-five degrees, and in winter, cold, wet winds off the sea.
t.boszhira@43.4,54.1:
Boszhira is a landscape that looks like it was designed for a science-fiction film and then abandoned. In the Mangystau desert, on the edge of the Ustyurt plateau, wind and water have carved the pale chalk and clay into towers, ridges, amphitheatres and the famous jagged teeth that stand over a wide, empty basin. The colours change through the day, from dead white at noon to orange and pink in the evening. The rocks here were once the floor of an ancient sea, and fossil shells can still be found.

Reaching it is a journey. From Aktau, the main highway runs across a flat, stony plain for a long way, with trucks, heat and distance, and then you leave the pavement for tracks that vary from hard-packed clay to soft sand and loose rock. A motorcycle with good tyres and some off-road skill is fine in dry weather, but rain can turn the clay slippery and sticky, and sandy sections can catch the unwary. Many people go with a guide or in a convoy of vehicles, which makes sense given the lack of help.

Out here, the silence is the main event. You will probably meet camels, a few herders and a sky that goes on forever. Summer heat can pass forty degrees, with almost no shade, so spring and autumn are far kinder. Winter nights are bitterly cold. Wind is steady and can be strong, and dust gets everywhere. It is wise to carry more water than seems sensible, a tow rope or tyre repair kit, and a satellite or spare communication device, since phone coverage fails in the hollows.

Shops and cafes along the main road are few, and the basics, such as water, food and shade, are your own responsibility. Camping is the standard way to stay. If you plan well and travel with respect, it is among the most unusual and memorable places a motorcycle can reach in Central Asia.
t.paso de jama point 4@-23.2,-67.0:
Beyond Susques the road enters one of the emptiest and highest stretches of the whole journey, the high Puna, where the plateau runs on at around four thousand metres and the horizon is a rim of volcanoes. The road climbs gently towards the Paso de Jama, which is at about 4,200 metres and is the main Argentine border crossing into the Atacama. There are no towns at these coordinates and nothing resembling services, so a full tank and a spare is the only sensible policy.

The landscape is stark and unforgettable. Salt flats, shallow lagoons dyed pink by algae and flamingos, and bare mountains in shades of brown, red and grey lie in all directions. Vicunas graze on the sparse grass, and sometimes a fox or a rhea darts across the road. The sky is a deep, dark blue and the sunlight is fierce, so protect your skin and eyes. At night, the stars are astonishing, but the temperature falls well below freezing.

Riding here is mostly straight, steady and fast, with long views and sparse traffic, mainly trucks heading to and from Chile. The surface is generally good but can be damaged by frost and flood. Altitude plays tricks on both bike and rider: fuel injection can be rich or lean, and breathing, concentration and reaction time all suffer. Ride within your limits, pause often, and drink water. Headaches and nausea are signs to descend.

Weather is a serious risk. Wind, snow and ice can appear at any time of year, and the road can be closed by storms, sometimes for days. Border hours also matter, and the crossing can be shut in poor weather, so check before you commit. The best time is the dry season from April to October, but the cold in winter is severe. If you plan to continue, remember that the border formalities are done at a complex before the pass, with customs, immigration and agricultural checks, so bring patience and all your documents.
